A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaptGrad work despite the changed title. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. All post-reference Sections 7–13 in v2 were inspected; v1 ends with references and contains no appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original out-of-bounds sampling measurements, saliency visualizations, and quantitative MNIST/ImageNet evaluations in Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v2 reports original saliency evaluations and additional correlation, sensitivity, clipping, localization, adversarial-generation and runtime experiments, including appendix results.

M1.justification: Gradient averaging, diagonal Gaussian covariance and the confidence-dependent distance-to-boundary sampling rule remain unchanged between v1 Equations 11–13 and v2 Equations 10–12. The explicit zero scale at boundary pixels in v2 was already implied by v1's formula. ClipGrad is an added comparator, not a modification of AdaptGrad.

E1.justification: MNIST and ImageNet are retained, but v2 adds object localization and pixel-level adversarial example generation in Section 11. Section 13 also introduces targeted evaluations on extreme-contrast, small-object, large-object and multiple-object images, substantially broadening task and scenario coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds the clipping-based ClipGrad comparator in Tables 8–9. It omits NG, S-NG and A-NG from the reported consistency/invariance comparison that included them in v1 Table 1. The main Grad, SmoothGrad, GI, IG and NoiseGrad comparison families otherwise remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds insertion/deletion faithfulness AUC evaluation with 5% pixel batches and zero filling, quantitative sampling/scale parameter grids, and new downstream protocols. These include selective-search localization precision and pixel-level FGSM evaluation targeting class probability below 0.5. These are substantial new evaluation procedures; the retained MLP training configuration is unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 expands the earlier sampling-count/confidence illustrations with quantitative parameter sensitivity, a ClipGrad control, and contrast/object-size case studies. Its bias experiment and OBA/OBV correlation analysis investigate the proposed noise mechanism, replacing v1's simpler aggregate out-of-bounds measurements and Gaussian-tail illustration.

E5.justification: Although v1 includes uncertainty for its out-of-bounds measurements, its principal benchmark tables contain point estimates. v2 newly specifies five independent experiments and reports means and variances, adds Spearman tests with p-values, and reports ten independent adversarial experiments with a distribution plot. This establishes expanded statistical reporting, not an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Reported VGG16 SG/AG sparseness changes from 0.5334/0.5608 in v1 Table 2 to 0.5289/0.5740 in v2 Table 3; v2 Table 6 retains the earlier default-setting pair, so a same-setting gain is not established. Numerous correlation, faithfulness, clipping, localization, attack and runtime results are added. The earlier Information Level scores largely reappear as SIC in Table 7, with VGG16 IG(W) changing from 0.5635 to 0.5636.

T1.justification: The central convolution and Gaussian-tail derivations remain substantively unchanged. Section 12 adds a brief asymptotic-cost argument deriving linear input-dimension work for adaptive scale construction. The explicit boundary case and standard Gini formula otherwise clarify existing mathematics rather than introduce new theoretical results.

C1.justification: The main claims of efficient, broadly applicable gradient denoising persist. v2 shifts the abstract's emphasis from convolution reinterpretation toward sampling-induced extra noise, and its conclusion explicitly claims superiority in robustness, extending v1's characterization of AdaptGrad as a qualified alternative.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations concerning clipping artifacts, noise influencing deletion scores, and potential localization/adversarial applications. It explicitly acknowledges that indirect noise measurements may inadequately establish the proposed mechanism and discusses faithfulness limitations. Conversely, v1's limitation concerning the Gaussian kernel's shortest-edge construction is removed.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an explicit code-repository address and substantial reproducibility information in Sections 7–12: benchmark subset size, metric implementations, IG/NG settings, hardware, memory recommendations, downstream algorithm parameters and measured execution times. These additions largely document previously unspecified implementation choices rather than establish changes to existing experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds seven references, including Smoothed Geometry for Robust Attribution, selective search and additional attribution/application methods. Section 3.1 now explicitly attributes the convolution interpretation to prior work. The related-work taxonomy and central relationship to SmoothGrad remain largely intact.

P1.justification: v2 extensively edits existing prose across the abstract, introduction, mathematical exposition and evaluation sections, changes the title and author block, and revises noise terminology. It also reorganizes metric discussion and supporting explanations into dedicated post-reference sections and substantially rewrites the limitations discussion.

P2.justification: The combined cross-model results table becomes three dense model-specific tables, with earlier Information Level results separately displayed as SIC. Figure 2 is recomposed, the Gaussian-tail diagram is replaced by a bias experiment, and numerous sensitivity, localization, adversarial and scenario displays are added. Retained visualizations are also resized or relocated.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the implementation details, repeated-run reporting, clipping control and sensitivity tests make v2 easier to reproduce and assess. However, the added evidence is overinterpreted: Table 1 correlations are very weak, deletion scores in Tables 3–5 favor SmoothGrad despite broad faithfulness claims, and Table 7 retains a counterexample to the claimed consistent SIC superiority. These problems temper the benefits of the expanded evaluation.
